stem: A hospital's adult blood-culture contamination rate decreases after a standardized collection initiative. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: Fewer cultures are being classified as probable contaminants, which supports improved collection quality and reduces the risk of false-positive results leading to unnecessary antibiotics.
options.B: The lower contamination rate proves that all bloodstream infections are now being detected correctly and no other collection-quality measures are needed.
options.C: The rate is unrelated to preanalytic collection practices and therefore has little value for quality improvement.
options.D: A lower contamination rate means fewer true bloodstream infections are being diagnosed and indicates that cultures should be collected less carefully.

rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies blood-culture contamination rate as a patient-safety and laboratory-quality measure used to monitor collection practices. Contamination by skin commensals can produce false-positive results that lead to unnecessary antibiotic therapy and prolonged hospitalization. CDC states that monitoring contamination and single-set rates helps reveal gaps in blood-culture collection and supports improvement of standardized practices. B overclaims what one quality metric can prove. C contradicts CDC's quality-measure purpose. D confuses contamination with true bacteremia.
educational_objective: Interpret a lower blood-culture contamination rate as evidence of fewer probable contamination events and improved collection quality, while recognizing that contamination monitoring does not by itself prove perfect bloodstream-infection detection.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Division of Laboratory Systems
source_document_title: Prevent Adult Blood Culture Contamination; Primary Measure: Blood Culture Contamination Rate; Report and Take Action
source_version_date: CDC quality-tool pages current through March 31, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Prevent Adult Blood Culture Contamination — Why it is important: skin commensals can cause false-positive cultures leading to unnecessary antibiotic therapy and prolonged hospitalization; best practices improve diagnosis and reduce contamination. Primary Measure — Overview: BCC rate calculates the relative incidence of contaminated blood cultures and is important for maintaining quality practices. Report and Take Action — monitoring BCC and single-set rates provides insight into collection practices and reveals gaps requiring mitigation.
source_claim_supported: Blood-culture contamination rate is a quality measure of probable contamination events and collection practices; reducing contamination reduces false-positive risk and avoidable antibiotic exposure, but the metric does not prove complete diagnostic accuracy by itself.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: maintain specimen integrity, use proper infection-related collection practices, and participate in safety/quality improvement.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — blood-culture contamination quality monitoring
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw item to avoid claiming that a lower contamination rate specifically proves better skin antisepsis alone. The final item uses CDC's broader, directly supported interpretation: fewer probable contaminants, better collection quality, and less false-positive-driven antibiotic exposure.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against CDC's current March 2026 adult blood-culture contamination quality tool.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reflects the measure's purpose and downstream false-positive harm. B incorrectly treats one metric as proof of complete diagnostic accuracy. C denies the documented preanalytic-quality relationship. D confuses contamination reduction with reduced true bacteremia detection.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; fewer probable contaminants and improved collection quality.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; contamination rate is not a complete diagnostic-performance measure.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; CDC explicitly uses it to assess collection quality.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; contamination is not true bloodstream infection.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A makes the appropriately bounded inference supported by CDC.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same quality metric rather than unrelated bedside procedures.
audit_findings.blueprint: Specimen quality and infection-related safety improvement fit Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked whether lower contamination can be attributed specifically to antisepsis, staff technique, collection device, or other factors. The final wording avoids single-cause attribution and limits the inference to fewer probable contaminants and improved collection quality. No second answer remained.
